newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Ad agency predicts future trends.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Ad agency predicts future trends.

text.p: Nostalgia, classic brands and alcoholic drinks that "don't give you a hangover" are going to be big consumer trends in the future," an American expert told Reuters on Tuesday.
Marian Salzman is one of a growing brand of professional "futurologists" who spend their time predicting how we will live our lives after the millennium.

Salzman, who works for TBWA ad agency and has the unusual job title of heading TBWA's "Department of the Future", regularly contacts large numbers of trend-setting consumers whom she believes are at the cutting edge of fashion.
These consumers help Salzman to predict what the not-so-fashion-conscious consumers in western countries will be doing in the next few years.
"I use these consumers to track trends for clients, so that they can be prepared for the future," she said.
Salzman said the theme of nostalgia would play a big role in the future.

"People will look back to an era when they felt safer and more secure so adults will start collecting things such as Pez (confectionery dispensers) that they associate with their childhoods," she says.
Salzman was in London on one of her frequent trips from TBWA in Amsterdam. TBWA is part of TBWA/Chiat Day ad agency in the United States, which is owned by Omnicom Group Inc.
Salzman predicts that middle class consumers will increasingly crave classic brands in the next five years.

"As life becomes more scary and confusing, this middle group of consumers will turn to things like Campbell's or Heinz soups -- brands that they grew up with and which give them a warm fuzzy feeling," she said.

Salzman also predicts the fast-changing pace of technology will mean that as well as classic brands, consumers will also be able to buy "smart products" such as alcohol that does not give you a hangover, specially packaged food for the elderly which contains all the vitamins and minerals they need and "nutraceuticals", or food which also has medicinal benefits.
Time will become an increasingly valuable commodity and will be treasured as professionals are overloaded with information either in the form of e-mail, faxes or via the Internet.
"People will want to use their leisure time to unwind. Solitude will be important so I think people will need spaces where they can go to be alone."

Salzman said that those consumers who can afford it will pamper themselves. "Spas will become increasingly popular not for holidays but as one day treats and I also think we will see a growing number of oxygen bars."

The world's first "oxygen spa bar" opened in Toronto last year. Instead of alcohol, customers are served pure oxygen via a tube which allows them to chat to other customers and drink organic fruit juices.
Salzman said that the future will not just belong to young people.
"An important group of consumers will be what I call the oldest olds -- people of 80 plus who still feel well and have money to enjoy themselves."
She said there were already signs that this age group were spending a significant amount of money on luxuries such as holidays and even cars.

"Car manufacturers will have to consider what this will mean to them. They may have to redesign cars so that they are easier to get in and out of if they are to successfully target this market," said Salzman.
While the future may look bright for those with money it is a different story for those at the bottom of the economic heap, she said.
For those without financial means, consuming will become a matter of instant gratification.
"Those with no jobs and with a sense of hopelessness will want everything in an instant such as super-strength alcoholic drinks that will get them drunk very quickly."
Salzman says that the children of this group of consumers will also be an underclass. "They will become technological have-nots and without technological skills they will not progress."
She said that evidence suggests this group will feel disengaged from society and that anger, rage and violence will increase in American and European inner cities.
Salzman said she expected some cynics to dismiss her predictions as fantasy, but she added: "I have got it right in the past."
Industry experts have credited her with identifying a growing number of Western consumer trends.
She said: "I was the person who identified "wiggers" -- white teenagers who wanted to be black and adopt black street fashion styles, which then spawned a whole industry for baggy clothing."
And a growing number of companies including Levi's, Coca-Cola and Kodak are now seeking her advice.
